1:
The heading needs qualifying before it can be used, and each witness qualifies it differently. Gill rules out two readings: the phrase points not back to the psalm of the preceding chapter but forward, and cannot mean the last words David ever spoke, since the advice to Solomon and the temple instructions came later. He settles on either the last after the book of Psalms was finished or the last delivered under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. Wesley takes the second, that these are not simply the last he spoke but the last he spake by the Spirit of God, assisting and directing him extraordinarily. Clarke narrows it to form, supposing the last poetical composition to be meant — David might have spoken many words after these in prose, but none in verse — and says plainly that other meanings are given and this is the one he prefers.

Whether the piece counts as prophecy is contested, and Gill reports the dispute rather than settling it. The Jewish authorities, he says, will not allow David the spirit of prophecy: they own he spoke by the Holy Spirit, which they distinguish from prophecy. Against that he sets the Targum, which calls the words a prophecy outright and takes them for a prophecy of the Messiah, paraphrasing them as what David prophesied concerning the end of the world and the days of consolation to come. Clarke reads the song the same way, finding in it a glorious prediction of the Messiah's kingdom and conquests in highly poetic language. Gill adds why the heading is there — to excite attention, the last words of dying men being usually regarded and remembered.

Both the grammatical commentators anchor the opening to Balaam. Keil and Delitzsch hold that the introduction rests, in form and in substance, upon Balaam's last sayings concerning the future history of Israel (Numbers 24:3; Numbers 24:15), which shows how far David had occupied himself with what earlier men of God said of Israel's future, and indicates that his own utterance was meant to expand Balaam's prophecy of the Star out of Jacob and the Sceptre out of Israel; like Balaam, he calls it an oracle. Ellicott reaches the parallel through a single word, noting that the term rendered said, used twice here, is a peculiar form employed some two to three hundred times of direct Divine utterances and applied to human sayings only here, in those passages of Numbers, and in Proverbs 30:1 — in every one of which a special claim to inspiration is being made.

The two titles are read as a pair, the one low and the other high. Henry takes the son of Jesse for the meanness of David's origin, and draws the lesson that it is good for those advanced to be corner-stones and top-stones to remind themselves of the rock out of which they were hewn; Wesley glosses the raising up as advancement from an obscure estate to the kingdom, God having singled him out from all the families of Israel. Henry distributes the remaining titles by office: as the anointed of the God of Jacob David served his people in their civil interests, and as the sweet psalmist in their religious exercises, penning the psalms, setting the tunes, and appointing both the singers and the instruments. Ellicott renders that title literally as he that is pleasant in Israel's psalms, earned by the composition and arrangement of Israel's liturgical songs, and argues that David sends the song to posterity with just such a description of its writer as would secure its authority. Clarke extends the title past Israel, making him the sweet psalmist of every part of the habitable world where religion and piety have been held in reverence. Wesley alone questions the voice, judging these to be not David's own words but those of the sacred penman of the book.
2:
The claim advanced here concerns the origin of what David uttered, and Gill takes it to reach back over everything he ever composed. The psalms and songs were not fruits of his own genius but were set down under the breathing of God's Spirit, by whom the holy men who served as penmen of Scripture spoke exactly as they were moved — David among them, in the character of a prophet. Gill cites the Targum to the same effect, that the king delivered these things by the spirit of prophecy; and he offers a second construction of the preposition, on which the Spirit spoke within him, so that the saying was impressed inwardly upon the mind before ever it reached the tongue — internal in its origin and only outward in its delivery.

Clarke divides the sentence and refuses to let either half absorb the other. From the opening he infers that the substance of the writing arrived by direct and immediate inspiration; from the clause about the tongue, that the words of this writing were as directly inspired as the matter of it. The verse furnishes a separate ground for each — the Spirit having spoken through him, and God's utterance having rested upon his mouth — so that on Clarke's account David was not merely handed a topic but granted the phrasing of it. Ellicott reaches the same destination by a shorter road, observing that in keeping with the preceding sentence this clause and the one beside it assert as plainly as possible that the whole came under the prompting and guidance of the Divine Spirit.

Wesley widens the scope backwards across the psalter. What follows here, and by extension the other compositions uttered on comparably solemn occasions, is on no account to be reckoned a human invention, since matter and diction alike were suggested by the Spirit — whom Wesley styles the great teacher of the church. Taken together with Clarke, the sentence therefore performs two offices at once: it certifies the oracle about to be spoken, and it vouches retrospectively for the collection of songs the dying king was leaving to his people.
3:
The speaker is named twice, and the titles are read for what they guarantee. Gill takes the God of Israel to be the covenant God of Israel literally considered, and also the covenant God and Father of the whole spiritual Israel. On the second title the witnesses diverge: Clarke makes the Rock the Fountain whence Israel was derived, Wesley makes it the strength and defence and protector of his people — manifested, he adds, in God's directing kings and rulers so to manage their power as may most conduce to their people's comfort and benefit — while Ellicott reads it as a guarantee of reliability, a frequent Scriptural comparison (2 Samuel 22:3) and appropriate here to show the perfect dependability of what God declares.

What follows is grammatically open, and the three readings of it are genuinely different. Ellicott concedes that the original is exceedingly elliptical both here and in the next verse, but holds the English gives the true sense, and calls this the most perfect statement ever made of the fundamental point of all just government — that it must be in the fear of God. Wesley reads the clause as a job description, finding in it the two principal parts of a king's duty answerable to the two tables of God's law, justice towards men and piety towards God. Clarke renders it as an identification rather than a requirement: more literally, he that ruleth in man is the just one, or the just one is the ruler among men — and he applies it directly: it is by God's fear that Christ rules the hearts of all his followers, and the man without the fear of God before his eyes can never be a Christian.

Keil and Delitzsch rule out one construction of the next verse on grounds of theology rather than grammar. The proposal is to join the two verses into a single period, so that the sense becomes: when one rules justly over men, as I do, it is as when a morning becomes clear. This they reject for a stated reason — it overlooks Nathan's promise (2 Samuel 7:12) altogether, and weakens the force of a saying so solemnly introduced as the word of God. The ruler David sees in spirit is therefore not simply anyone who rules righteously, and on their reading the verse describes the blessing that will proceed from that ruler.

Who the figure of light is meant to be divides the rest. Clarke calls the verse very obscure, since it does not appear from it who the person spoken of is, and settles on the Messiah as probably intended because the Messiah seems to be the whole subject of these last words; he notes that one of Kennicott's manuscripts supplies the divine name, which would yield the reading that as the light of the morning ariseth Jehovah. Gill applies the metaphors first to any ruler who rules in righteousness and the fear of God, whose administrations promise a growing happiness like the morning light with no forebodings of dark times, and then to Christ as the true light, the morning star, the dayspring from on high and the sun of righteousness — the first discovery of whom to Adam, after sin had brought a night of darkness on the world, was as the dawn. Ellicott ties the picture to Nathan's promise and to Psalms 72, and argues that David knew far too much of the evil of his own heart and of the troubles in his household to suppose his ideal could be realised in any descendant but the one who should crush the serpent's head. Wesley alone keeps the verse on the king: a duty to rule not only with justice and piety but with sweetness, gentleness and condescension to his people's infirmities, rendering his government as acceptable as sunshine in a clear morning.
5:
Taken as a concession, the opening clause is an admission about David's own family, and Gill offers three senses for it. The house may be not so bright and flourishing as the government of the just ruler just described; or not right with God, meaning the family in which great sins were committed and great disorders brought in, as the cases of Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah showed; or not firm and stable, through the rebellion of one son, the insurrection of another and the usurpation of a third. Wesley reads it the same way and makes the admission explicit: God knows that neither David nor his children had lived and ruled as they should have done, so justly and in the fear of the Lord, and that they had therefore not enjoyed the uninterrupted prosperity they might have had.

The grammatical commentators will not have the concessive reading at all. Keil and Delitzsch hold that the first and last clauses can only be made to yield a sense in harmony with the context by being taken as questions — is not my house so with God? — the interrogation being indicated only by the tone, as frequently happens elsewhere (Hosea 11:5; Malachi 2:15). Clarke arrives at the same place by a change of vowels, reading the word not as so but as established, and taking the whole verse as an interrogation that carries a positive assertion: is not my house established with God, because he hath made with me an everlasting covenant? On his account the sense then becomes at once clear and consistent.

Ellicott sets the two options side by side and then declines the fashionable one. The verse is extremely difficult and admits of two interpretations: the rendering in the English, which he notes is also that of the Septuagint, the Vulgate and the Syriac, makes David recognise how far he and his house have failed to realise the ideal just set forth, while holding that since God's promise is sure it must be realised in his posterity. Most modern commentators, he reports, prefer instead to take the clauses interrogatively. His own judgment is that the Hebrew admits either rendering, but that the reading of the ancient versions gives a higher idea of David's spiritual discernment — so the weight of recent opinion is acknowledged and set aside.

On the covenant itself there is no disagreement, and each of its terms gets pressed. Keil and Delitzsch tie the whole oracle back to its source, the prophecy of the just ruler being sustained by being traced to the original promise in which David had received his pledge. Wesley reads that promise as continuing the kingdom to David and his seed for ever (2 Samuel 7:16) until the coming of the Messiah, who is to be his son and successor and whose kingdom shall have no end — granted notwithstanding all the transgressions by which they had broken covenant, and by a God to whom all his sins were known. Ellicott glosses the covenant as ordered in all like a carefully drawn legal document, providing for all contingencies and leaving no room for misconstruction; Wesley takes the same word of God's eternal counsel and providence, which will overrule even the sins of David's house so far that though he punish them he will not utterly root them out. On the closing clause both Gill and Clarke read a deferral rather than a doubt: Gill expects the house to be firm and stable in the Messiah who should spring from him, and Clarke holds that all is sure with respect to his spiritual successor though that successor does not yet appear, the covenant being firm and certain to spring forth in due time.
6:
The oracle turns to the opposite of the flourishing it has just described, and the contrast is drawn in the figure itself. Gill makes the point by setting the two images against each other: not the tender grass that springs up and flourishes after rain and sunshine, but thorns, useless and hurtful and fit only for burning. He applies it at two levels — to wicked men in general, who cast off the yoke of the Lord and become unprofitable, which he notes is what the name itself signifies; and to wicked governors in particular, who instead of being helpful are harmful to a commonwealth, and instead of being the joy of their subjects give pain and trouble, and are, if possible, to be thrust away and deposed. Wesley reads the turn structurally, as the account of the enemies of a kingdom whose nature and stability the preceding verses had settled.

Two witnesses press the grammar of the name. Ellicott observes that according to the Masoretic punctuation the word stands not in its common form but in the stronger abstract form, meaning worthlessness itself; Keil and Delitzsch say the same and draw the consequence, that the abstract is stronger than the phrase worthless man and depicts the godless as personified worthlessness. Clarke notes that there is no word for sons in the text at all, only the good-for-nothing man, and suggests the reference may be first to Saul and secondly to the enemies of Christ. Ellicott states the principle he thinks the verse rests on, that the coming in of Divine righteousness leads not only to the assimilation of what is holy but also to the rejection of what is evil, by a law as necessary and immutable as that of action and reaction in the material world.

What sort of thorns are meant is settled by how they are handled. Keil and Delitzsch insist the epithet applies to the ungodly rather than to the thorns, and that the reference is to thorns men root out, not to those they avoid on account of their prickles — the proof being that to clear the ground of them a man does not lay hold with the bare hand. Gill reports two constructions of the arming: either weapons of war must be used to conquer and destroy them, which he traces to Ben Gersom and De Dieu, or a man who meddles with them must expect to be as wounded as if the spear's handle and not merely its iron head were thrust into him. Gill prefers the former.

Clarke alone reads the whole figure as a piece of ordinary craft. The metaphor is taken from hedging: the workman thrusts the thorns aside with his bill or with a hand protected by an impenetrable glove until, getting a fair blow at the roots, he cuts them all down — the man fenced with iron and the handle of his bill like the staff of a spear. Clarke identifies the implement as the dubbing-bill with a handle five or six feet long, used to slash a thorn hedge on each side before the tops are levelled, and calls the image perfectly natural and intelligible. Ellicott describes the same tool more briefly as an iron hook on the end of a spear staff, but is candid about the final phrase: used only here, its meaning is quite uncertain, the Vulgate rendering it to utter destruction and the Septuagint substituting the word shame, with the English rendering as well sustained as any.
8:
Ellicott accounts for the position: a list of David's chief heroes belongs naturally in the summary closing his reign. A duplicate with several variations and sixteen further names stands in 1 Chronicles 11:10-47, each list useful for correcting the clerical errors in the other. He cautions that neither list belongs to any definite time, being rather a catalogue of those who distinguished themselves at any point in David's life. Wesley agrees the catalogue, though placed here, was taken long before, which he thinks manifest from Asahel and Uriah being named in it. Henry assigns the record four purposes: the honour of David, who trained these men and set them an example of conduct and courage; the honour of the worthies who brought him to the crown and enlarged his conquests; the exciting of later generations to emulation; and the showing how much religion contributes to true courage. Wesley draws that last conclusion in nearly the same words — when they became famous for piety, they became famous for bravery (1 Chronicles 29:6).

The corps has a structure, and one conspicuous absence. Gill sets out three classes: the first and highest of three only, who were general officers; the second also of three, perhaps colonels of regiments; and the third of thirty, captains of thousands and hundreds. Both Gill and Ellicott notice Joab is nowhere in it, Ellicott explaining that as commander-in-chief he stood in a rank by himself. Keil and Delitzsch fasten on the heading, where this text has the names of the mighty men and the Chronicles their number — striking, since Chronicles gives no total at the close as this one does. They reject Bertheau's copyist's error for the word meaning selection, and explain the reading from the corps having been named for the number it originally consisted of. Ellicott adds that the word for captain and the word for three are much alike, so the text here and in Chronicles perpetually fluctuates between them.

The first hero's name is agreed to be damaged. Keil and Delitzsch take the form here to be unquestionably spurious against the Chronicles reading, and follow Kennicott's conjecture that it arose from two letters of the true name being written beneath the neighbouring word. Clarke gives it as Jashobeam the Hachmonite, and Ellicott concurs, adding that he came to David at Ziklag (1 Chronicles 12:1) and afterwards became general of the first division of the army (1 Chronicles 27:2). Henry observes how little else survives: he cannot recall reading of any of these men or their actions anywhere in David's story except here and in the parallel chapter, many remarkable events being passed over in the annals.

On the rest of the verse the emenders and the harmoniser part. Clarke reports Kennicott's finding of three corruptions in this one verse — the hero's proper name turned into two common words, the phrase he lifted up his spear turned into two proper names wholly inadmissible here, and eight hundred standing where three hundred was probably original. Kennicott's measure of the absurdity is that making Jashobeam the Hachmonite the same man as Adino the Eznite is nearly as bad as making David the Bethlehemite the same as Elijah the Tishbite. Clarke adds a lexical reduction of the feat: the word rendered slain should probably be soldiers, as the Septuagint has it, so the man withstood three hundred at one time. Ellicott agrees the disputed words yield no meaning in their connection and are generally considered a corruption. Wesley holds the opposite: Adino was the man's proper name, and the differences between the lists are reconciled by one person having divers names and by some worthies dying and others coming in their stead. He lets the number stand too, judging eight hundred in one battle not incredible in a man of extraordinary strength whose enemies were discouraged and fleeing.
9:
The second of the first class is placed by rank rather than by sequence. Gill reads the phrase after him as meaning the next to the Tachmonite, the second worthy of the first class, and Keil and Delitzsch gloss it the same way, as next to him in rank. On the father's name the two forms are treated as one: Ellicott notes that the Hebrew margin and the Chronicles give Dodo while the text here gives Dodai, as does the passage where he appears as the general for the second month (1 Chronicles 27:4), and holds the name the same under slightly differing forms. Keil and Delitzsch resolve another variation the same way: where this text has the son of an Ahohite the Chronicles has the Ahohite, and they refuse to strike the word out as spurious, since the son of an Ahohite is the same thing as the Ahohite. Both Gill and Ellicott trace the patronymic to Ahoah, a descendant of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:4).

The setting of the exploit is where the text is weakest, and Ellicott reconstructs it. The words translated there gathered require the mention of some place that this text does not supply, and the construction of the verb rendered defied is unusual; the parallel passage reads instead that he was with David at Pas-dammim, and there the Philistines were gathered. Ellicott judges the difference between the two readings small in the original and the latter better, and identifies the place with the Ephes-dammim of 1 Samuel 17:1, where Goliath defied the armies of Israel and was slain by David. Clarke reaches the same battle by a different route, supposing the defiance here to refer to the war in which David slew Goliath.

A second correction follows from the first. Ellicott argues that the clause rendered were gone away should be were gathered to battle, as the Septuagint, Vulgate and Syriac all translate it and as the Hebrew requires; and he explains the error's origin, that in the Chronicles the battle in which Shammah was engaged is omitted altogether, so that the notice of the people fleeing before the Philistines became attached to this engagement instead, Josephus following that text. Wesley takes the English as it stands, glossing gone away as fled away, being dismayed at the approach of their enemies — which leaves the two readings pointing opposite ways on whether the army advanced or ran.

What Eleazar then did is reported with one striking physical detail. Gill has him rise up when the Israelites fled, stand his ground alone, and fight the Philistines with his sword until his hand was weary with smiting. Ellicott takes the clause about the hand cleaving to the sword literally and defends it from experience, noting that instances are rare but well authenticated of a sort of cramp following excessive exertion, in which the hand could only be released from the weapon by external appliances. On the people returning after him he removes a possible slur: the phrase does not imply that they had at any time deserted him, but only that they turned wherever he went, to gather the spoil of the men he had slain.
11:
The third of the first class is placed, like the second, by rank. Gill names him the third of the first three and derives the patronymic from the country, following the Targum in taking it of the mountainous region — the hill country of Judea, of Hebron or the parts adjacent — and notes that a man of the same name appears among the thirty. Keil and Delitzsch treat the form here as a contraction of the longer form that occurs later in the list, and introduce him as the third leading hero, made renowned like the others by a great victory over the Philistines.

How the enemy had gathered turns on a word with two possible vowel-pointings. Keil and Delitzsch take it as a troop or crowd, a sense they say is thoroughly established from the Arabic, though it seems to have fallen into disuse afterwards, the Chronicles explaining it in two later places by the ordinary words for battle and camp. Ellicott records that Josephus, using different vowels, read it as a place name — Lehi, the scene of Samson's exploit (Judges 15:9) — but argues the English reading should be retained, since the same word recurs a little further on clearly in the sense of troop.

What grew in the field is disputed and then declared not to matter. Clarke notes that where this text has lentiles the Chronicles has barley, and judges one of the two Hebrew words a probable mistake for the other; he reports the suggestion that both crops stood in the field, that a marauding party of Philistines came to destroy or carry them off, and that these worthies defeated the whole and saved the produce, which he calls not unlikely. Wesley proposes the same solution and extends it, since the Chronicles ascribes the exploit to Eleazar while implying he had partners — so Eleazar might have fought where the barley was and Shammah where the lentiles were. Ellicott cuts the question short: the two words might easily be confounded and it is quite immaterial which is correct, the point being that the Philistines had made a foray to gather the ripe crops, that the Israelites were terrified and fled, and that Shammah by his courage turned the tide of battle.

The exploit itself is briefly told and the credit carefully assigned. Gill locates the stand precisely, in the midst of the field of lentiles. The verse gives the victory to the LORD rather than to the man, and Wesley presses the distinction: however great the bravery of the instruments, the praise of the achievement is to be given to God — these fought, but God wrought the victory. Keil and Delitzsch read the next notice as a deliberate pairing, a similar heroic feat appended to this one and performed by three of the thirty whose names are not given.
13:
Which three went down is left open by the text, and three answers are offered. Gill reports that some understand the three already named, Josephus among them, on the view that having related particular exploits of theirs the historian now records one in which all were concerned; others take the three who come next, Abishai chief, Benaiah second and Asahel third. Gill prefers the first of these. Keil and Delitzsch argue the opposite from the grammar: because the numeral carries no article here or in the Chronicles, the three intended are not Jashobeam, Eleazar and Shammah but three others from the list that follows. Ellicott agrees on the same ground and names his candidates, another three more eminent than the rest of the thirty, two of them no doubt Abishai and Benaiah.

The number itself is treated as a corruption and as a title. Both Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott record that the written text reads thirty where three is required, a manifest error corrected in the margin and by the Chronicles. On what the thirty were, Ellicott takes the word for a common name for this band, perhaps originally exactly thirty but varying from time to time, the total at the end of the chapter standing at thirty-seven. Clarke makes the word an office rather than a count, noting that it can scarcely be said with propriety that we have thirty-seven out of thirty, still less with the sixteen added in the Chronicles, and pointing out that the same term is used of the captains over Pharaoh's chariots (Exodus 14:7).

Two smaller details are queried. Ellicott passes on Kirkpatrick's doubt about the time, that the preposition does not mean in and that the Chronicles reading to the rock is perhaps the true one. Clarke identifies the campaign rather than the season, taking this to be the same war spoken of earlier in the book (2 Samuel 5:17), with the Philistines encamped in the valley of Rephaim.

Where David was is given two locations. Gill offers the strong hold of Zion, on Josephus's authority, or else one on a rock near the cave of Adullam. Keil and Delitzsch set the scene as the text gives it — David on the mountain fortress, a troop of Philistines encamped in the valley, and a Philistine post then holding Bethlehem — which is what makes the well unreachable and the longing that follows a military problem rather than a domestic one.
15:
Every witness is careful that the longing was not an order. Gill supplies the circumstances — harvest time, the summer season, hot weather, and the king thirsty — and stresses that the three heard him express himself only in a general way, with no view that any should risk their lives. Clarke explains why this water in particular: Bethlehem was David's own city, he knew the excellence of the water there, and being near the place and parched with thirst it was natural for him to wish for a draught of it. Clarke is explicit that there is no evidence David requested it, the men having gone of their own accord and without his knowledge, and that they received no command from him at all. Wesley puts the same point from David's side, that he was far from desiring or expecting that any of his men should hazard their lives to procure it.

Whether the well still exists Ellicott reports as an open question. There are now no wells of living water at Bethlehem itself, the town being supplied by an aqueduct, and Robinson could find none in the neighbourhood and was assured that none existed; but Ellicott sets against this Ritter's statement that a little north of the town is David's well, with its deep shaft and its clear cool water. He leaves the two reports standing side by side rather than choosing between them.

The breakthrough is described as a passage through an army. Gill places the obstacle geographically, the host lying in the valley of Rephaim between the hold where David was and the well, so that the three had to make their way through it. Keil and Delitzsch narrow the obstacle to the outpost, holding that what the men broke through was the camp before the gate at Bethlehem. Ellicott reads the exploit for what it says about the man they did it for, since the act shows strikingly the personal power David had over his followers and the enthusiasm with which he inspired them.

Why he would not drink it is answered in four ways that do not cancel each other. Clarke's reason is the plainest — the men had got it at the hazard of their lives, so David considered it as their blood, and in refusing gave a noble instance of self-denial. Wesley puts the refusal as a calculation about appearances: by gratifying himself on such terms he would have seemed either to set too high a price on the satisfaction of his appetite or too low a price on the lives of his soldiers. On the pouring itself Ellicott notes that the verb used is the technical term for a sacrificial libation, so that David assimilated the act to a sacrifice by solemnly consecrating this dangerously won water. Keil and Delitzsch, citing Clericus, make the libation an act of thanksgiving — he poured it upon the earth, rendering God thanks for the return of the three brave men — while Wesley combines that with the sacred reading, taking it as a drink offering acknowledging God's goodness in preserving his captains in so dangerous an enterprise and as a sign that he esteemed the water a sacred thing not fit for him to drink. Clarke sets the whole scene beside a classical parallel, that libations of water and wine were frequent among the heathens, and recalls from Arrian how Alexander, when his army was oppressed with heat and thirst, sent back a cup of water with the words that he could not bear to drink alone while so many were in want and the cup was too small to divide among them all. Clarke calls the example noble in both cases, but adds that David put piety to his bravery, since he poured it out unto the Lord.
17:
The refusal is put as a question rather than a statement, and the form matters. Ellicott observes that the Hebrew here is simply an interrogative exclamation — the blood of the men? — while the Chronicles reads it out in full as a question whether he should drink the blood of these men, which is also how the Septuagint and Vulgate render the clause here. The force of the identification is then pressed: to David, water gained only at the risk of life seemed the very blood in which the life resides (Leviticus 17:11). Gill keeps to the plain sense of what was being declined, that he would not drink of the water these men had brought him. Keil and Delitzsch record the outcome in the verse's own terms, that he therefore would not drink it.

The closing summary is read as a hinge. Wesley takes the three to be named jointly here, with two of them then mentioned severally in the verses that follow. Ellicott corrects the article, preferring the three to these three, and Keil and Delitzsch mark the same point as a structural division, treating what follows as the heroes of the second class.

Abishai is introduced by his family and his command. Gill describes him as head of another triumvirate; Keil and Delitzsch identify him as Joab's brother (1 Samuel 26:6) and as chief of the body-guard, holding the same office as the first man in the earlier triad. Ellicott sets out the membership of this second group — the triad just mentioned, of whom Abishai was first, Benaiah second, and the third unnamed — and notes that a somewhat similar feat of daring is told of Abishai elsewhere, in the night raid on Saul's camp.

His exploit and his standing are reported in parallel clauses, and the second is textually damaged. Keil and Delitzsch describe the feat as swinging his spear over three hundred slain, and read the next clause as placing him by reputation among the three principal heroes of the first class. The words that follow, however, they say make no sense as written, and they take the numeral to be an error for the larger number, the thirty — pointing to the later verse which has it correctly in both texts, and explaining how the slip would have arisen from the similar word standing immediately before it. Ellicott notes the Hebrew margin reads the three in this clause and in the next, which leaves the same question of whether Abishai is being ranked among the three or set over the thirty.
19:
Abishai's rank is stated as a question with a limit attached. Gill answers the question affirmatively and adds the record it rests on: besides the exploit just told, Abishai went down with David into Saul's camp and took away the spear and cruse at his bolster, relieved David when in danger from the giant Ishbibenob, and beat the Edomites, slaying eighteen thousand of them in the valley of salt. The verse nonetheless withholds the highest rank from him, and Wesley reads the shortfall simply as a shortfall, that he fell short of the first three in strength and valour.

Benaiah is introduced through his father and his birthplace, and both are made to say something. Gill takes the father for a man of great vivacity, valour and strength, so that it was like father like son, and reports from Procopius Gazaeus the further claim that Benaiah was David's brother's son and a grandson of Jesse. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both identify the father with Jehoiada the priest (1 Chronicles 27:5) and raise the possibility that he is the Jehoiada who led the Aaronites to David at Hebron (1 Chronicles 12:27). Keil and Delitzsch note that the word describing him as a brave man is evidently defective here against the Chronicles. On the town, both place Kabzeel in the far south of Judah (Joshua 15:21), Ellicott adding that it lay on the border of Edom.

Ellicott traces the career the verse only hints at. Benaiah was general of the third division of the army, a command that probably included the Cherethites and Pelethites since he was also their commander (2 Samuel 8:18); and in consequence of his faithfulness to Solomon during the rebellion of Adonijah he was finally made commander-in-chief (1 Kings 2:35). Keil and Delitzsch give the same two commands from the earlier notices in this book.

What he killed is the chapter's most contested detail. Keil and Delitzsch read the phrase as the two Ariels of Moab and explain the title from usage, since the Arabs and Persians call every remarkably brave man a lion of God, so that these were two celebrated Moabite heroes; Ellicott gives the same literal rendering and the same usage among Arabs and Persians of great warriors. Clarke canvasses the alternatives without settling them — some think two real lions are meant, some two savage gigantic men, others two fortresses — and records that the Targum renders the phrase as the two princes of Moab. On the lion in the pit Ellicott is content to leave the method unknown: it is not said with what weapons Benaiah slew him, but the act was evidently a great feat of valour, and he points for comparison to David's own account of killing a lion as a shepherd (1 Samuel 17:34).
21:
The Egyptian's description is filled out from the parallel account. Ellicott explains the word rendered goodly by appeal to the Chronicles, where the man is termed one of stature and his height put at five cubits; Gill repeats that figure and reckons the difference, observing that he fell a cubit and a span short of Goliath. Clarke converts the measure, making five cubits about seven feet six inches. The exploit is therefore defined by a mismatch of equipment, which Ellicott states plainly: Benaiah closed with this giant carrying nothing but a staff, wrested the weapon from his grasp, and killed him with it.

Clarke alone asks whether such a thing is credible, and argues that it is. He reports having known men who, with a staff only for defence, could render useless the blade of the best practised soldier; and he recalls seeing one such person, set upon by a soldier with a hanger, beat the blade from his assailant's hand so completely that he might easily have despatched him with it. On that view the staff is no handicap the narrative invites us to admire, but an implement with real advantages against a thrusting arm.

He then lays a long classical parallel beside the verse, and its interest lies in the particulars. At Alexander's court a Macedonian named Horratas, proud of his military skill, treated a naked Athenian with contempt and challenged him for the following day. Horratas appeared accoutred at every point — a brazen shield and the long pike called a sarissa on his left arm, a javelin in his right hand, a sword belted at his side — while Dioxippus came crowned with a chaplet, a purple sash about one arm, his body bare and glistening with oil, and a club in his hand. Clarke, following his classical authority, has the javelin thrown from a distance and dodged by a sudden stoop; then, before the pike could be shifted across to the fighting hand, the Athenian sprang in and snapped it with a single stroke. Robbed of both shafts his opponent reached for the hilt, but Dioxippus closed, swept his feet from under him, flung him heavily down, planted a foot on his neck and drew the blade himself — and would have beaten out his brains had the king not intervened. The resemblance, Clarke concludes, is striking, and Benaiah appears to have been just such another clubsman.

The remaining two feats attract briefer notes. Wesley reads the pit as the circumstance that closed off every alternative, since there Benaiah lay under a necessity either of killing or of being killed, and takes the snow as an aggravation, lions being fiercest in cold seasons both from keenness of appetite and from scarcity of prey. Gill gathers the whole record into a line — a lion, two lion-like men of Moab, and an Egyptian of gigantic stature. Keil and Delitzsch add only the standing the verse confers, a name among the three mighty men.
23:
Benaiah's appointment is described by a phrase whose sense is argued over. Ellicott holds the word translated guard means rather private audience, so that David either made Benaiah a member of his council or set him over it, and he notes that if a name in one of the Chronicles lists is a transposition then the same office is recorded there too. Clarke reports the Vulgate's rendering, that David made him his privy counsellor, and gives the Hebrew idiom behind it — he put him to his ears, that is, confided his secrets to him. He adds a harsher possibility, that some think David made him a spy over the rest, and offers an aside on the fable that gave Midas very long ears, taking it to mean that the king had carried the system of espionage to a great length and kept a multitude of spies.

The verse also fixes his rank by subtraction rather than addition: Gill notes he was more honourable than the thirty whose names are recorded next, while the text still withholds the first three from him.

Asahel heads the third class, and his presence dates the list. Gill argues he was set over the thirty rather than counted among them, since thirty are reckoned besides him and the Arabic version calls him the prince of the thirty; and he repeats that Joab is not named at all, being general of the whole army and so not to be reckoned in any of the three classes. Ellicott reaches a chronological conclusion instead: because Asahel was killed by Abner while David reigned over Judah only (2 Samuel 2:23), the list plainly is not restricted to any one time in the reign — and he observes that leaving Asahel out, the names that follow come to exactly thirty. Clarke classes him with the officers or troops called by the disputed title he had discussed earlier.

From here the list runs through names about which there is not much to be said. Gill's note on the first is a scribal one, that Shammah the Harodite appears elsewhere as the Harorite through the frequent interchange of two similar letters, and Ellicott adds that he may be the same as a captain of the fifth division of the army and that the name following his is omitted in the Chronicles altogether. Clarke simply warns that several varieties occur in the names from this point, to be seen by comparing the two lists. Wesley states the principles he will apply throughout: the same names of persons and places are differently pronounced according to the dialects of different places and ages, one man often had two names, and David had more worthies than those named here — some of these having been killed early in his reign, as Asahel was, while others came up in their stead and still others were added, so that the Chronicles list names more men than this one numbers.
26:
Through this stretch of the list the commentators are mostly supplying one kind of fact, and it is an administrative one: almost every man named here turns out to have commanded one of the twelve monthly divisions of the army. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott between them assign Helez the seventh division, Ira the sixth, Abiezer the ninth, the man called Mebunnai here the eighth, and Maharai the tenth. The effect is to turn what reads as a roll of duellists into a list of standing officers, and to show that the catalogue of heroes and the rota of command were largely the same body of men under two descriptions.

The homes attached to the names are identified where they can be. Keil and Delitzsch take the first to be from Beth-pelet in the south of Judah (Joshua 15:27) and place Ira's Tekoah in the desert of Judah; Ellicott fixes the same town about six miles south of Bethlehem. On Anathoth both Gill and Ellicott note what it would later be famous for — Ellicott calling it a priestly city of Benjamin and both naming it the home of Jeremiah — while Keil and Delitzsch add its modern identification. The last of these notices is a family rather than a place: Gill derives the Ahohite from Ahoah, a grandson of Benjamin, and Keil and Delitzsch say the same, adding that nothing further is known of the man himself.

One location defeats them, and Keil and Delitzsch say so. Netophah is known from two later lists (Ezra 2:22; Nehemiah 7:26) to have been a place in the neighbourhood of Bethlehem, but it has not been discovered; and they rule out the obvious candidate, Beit Nattif, on the ground that it lies too far from Bethlehem. Of the man from it they can report only his tribal family and his division.

Three of the names in these verses cannot be settled at all, and the witnesses handle the three differently. The first man is a Paltite here and a Pelonite in both Chronicles passages; Keil and Delitzsch treat the latter as a misspelling in both places, while Gill reaches for the Targum, which makes the word a place name. The second is Mebunnai here and Sibbechai or Sibbecai elsewhere; Keil and Delitzsch call the form here simply a mistake in spelling, and Ellicott, who notes the two are the same in Hebrew and easily confused, identifies the man by his deed instead — he slew the giant Saph (2 Samuel 21:18). The third is Zalmon here and Ilai in the Chronicles, and here Keil and Delitzsch decline to adjudicate: which of the two names is the correct one, they say, it is impossible to decide. Ellicott records the variant without comment.
29:
Keil and Delitzsch pause over this run of names to say what the reader should expect of it: apart from Uriah at the very end, none of the men from here on is further known. What the commentary can supply is therefore limited to three things — a corrected spelling, a located birthplace, and occasionally a divisional command — and the interest lies in which of the three is available in each case.

The commands continue the rota noted earlier. Both Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott make the first man of these verses chief of the twelfth division, and both assign Benaiah the Pirathonite the eleventh — Ellicott adding the caution that he is of course to be distinguished from the Benaiah of the lion and the Egyptian. With that the sequence of monthly generals runs out, and the remaining names carry no office at all.

Several of the places can be put on a map, and two cannot. Keil and Delitzsch identify Pirathon in Ephraim with the village of Fer'ata to the south-west of Nablus, and Gill independently places it in Ephraim; they locate the Arbathite's home at Beth-haarabah or Arabah in the desert of Judah (Joshua 15:61), on the site of a ruin they name, while Gill is content to allow it to be in either Judah or Benjamin. Ellicott corrects the next epithet to the Baharumite, of the Bahurim mentioned earlier in the book (2 Samuel 16:5). The valleys of Gaash defeat them as Netophah did: Keil and Delitzsch put them in Ephraim by the mountain of that name but report the situation as not yet discovered, and of Shaalbon they say only that it may possibly survive in a modern village.

The spellings are corrected in different directions, which is worth noticing. Sometimes the Chronicles is preferred — Keil and Delitzsch hold the form here should be Cheled or Cheldai, and Ellicott records the name written three ways across the three lists. Sometimes this text is preferred: Keil and Delitzsch say the Chronicles writes Abi-Albon incorrectly as Abiel, where Ellicott takes the opposite view, that Abiel is probably correct and the extra syllable here crept in from the similar epithet on the line below. Elsewhere the difference is put down to a known scribal hazard, Ellicott explaining a variant by the frequent confusion of two letters. One pair of names, however, both agree is simply broken: Keil and Delitzsch judge the Chronicles text evidently the more correct, since the reading here does not make any sense, and they concede that because one of the names never occurs again there is a limit to what can be established about it.
32:
The first man here is located and the pair following him declared unusable. Gill puts Shaalbon in the tribe of Dan and wonders whether it answers to the Silbonitis of Josephus; Keil and Delitzsch propose that it may survive in a modern village (Joshua 19:42). What comes next they refuse to construe, holding that the words as they stand yield no sense and that the parallel register preserves the better text. Their candour about the limit deserves recording: since one of these words occurs nowhere else in Scripture, the most that can be established is that it must be written as a single word and therefore pointed otherwise than it is, and the locality it denotes remains simply unknown. They suspect too that the Shammah appearing in this stretch has drifted in from the earlier verse where it properly belongs.

Ellicott attacks the same difficulty with a copyist's explanation. He points out that the preposition rendered of has no warrant in the Hebrew and should be dropped, then offers two accounts of the troublesome phrase: either it duplicates by accident the last three letters of the word before it, or it forms part of the proper designation itself — in which case Jonathan stands alone, son of nobody named.

At the Hararite, Ellicott proposes a reconstruction with a consequence attached. A Shammah son of Agee the Hararite has already figured among the leading three, and the parallel register has here a Jonathan son of Shage; since Shage is nothing but Agee with a letter prefixed, Ellicott concludes that the true reading is probably Jonathan son of Shammah the Hararite. What follows is a family tie the roll would otherwise have hidden — Jonathan, one of the thirty, being son to one of the first three. He adds that the gentile epithet is spelt one way here, another in the clause immediately before, and a third in the parallel. Gill meanwhile preserves two older glosses of it: the Targum's, that it marks a man of the mountainous country, and the Arabic and Syriac, which make it the mount of Olives.

At the entry following, Keil and Delitzsch reason from the shape of the roll itself. Two heroes appear there where this text shows one, from which they conclude that a fusion has occurred; and they buttress it with two internal observations — that nowhere else in the whole roll is a man given both father and grandfather, and that the particle employed cannot properly precede a gentile noun. Their restoration accordingly splits the entry in two, yielding Eliphelet son of Ur and, separately, Hepher the Maachathite, of Maacah in north-eastern Gilead. Ellicott records the same divergence and leaves it unresolved. The closing designation draws most comment from both: Keil and Delitzsch make Eliam's father Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's clever but treacherous counsellor (2 Samuel 15:12), while Ellicott notes a wholly different man standing at this point in the parallel and judges two distinct persons probably intended, one preserved in either roll. His parting remark is that it is interesting to find a son of that counsellor numbered among David's thirty.
35:
Two of these homes sit close together in the hill country of Judah. Keil and Delitzsch place the Carmelite's Carmel in the mountains of Judah (1 Samuel 25:2) and the Arbite's Arab in the same region (Joshua 15:52); Ellicott fixes Carmel seven miles south-south-east of Hebron and remarks that it was famous in David's early history. Gill follows the Targum in reading the first epithet of Carmel or Carmela and notes the alternative form of the man's name. Where the two texts give different names outright, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree that it is impossible to decide which form is correct, though both think the Chronicles reading of the second man's patronymic an evident scribal error for the gentile name it closely resembles.

On the next pair the two commentators part company over which text to trust. Keil and Delitzsch judge that in all probability the Chronicles names are corrupt in this instance. Ellicott argues the opposite in detail, and his reconstruction is the more interesting for being mechanical rather than conjectural: the two forms of the first name differ in Hebrew by a single very similar letter; the description as brother rather than son may be resolved by manuscripts that read a compound name; and the apparently unrecognisable second entry resolves piece by piece, one word standing for the place name missing from the Chronicles, another for the man's name, and the last differing only by the frequently confused pair of letters. His conclusion is that the text here is the true one. Gill, for his part, simply records from Hillerus that the first man is the same as the one differently named elsewhere, and identifies Zobah as a kingdom in Syria.

A foreigner in the list draws comment from both sides. Gill offers four possibilities for the Ammonite — that he was one by birth and became a proselyte, as the Targum says; or was so called because he had sojourned in their land; or because he had done some exploits against them; or because he came from a town of that name in Benjamin. Ellicott treats the case as one of a class, grouping him with the Syrian of Zobah, Ittai the Gittite and Uriah the Hittite as foreigners who rose to distinction in David's service and were probably all proselytes.

The armour-bearer's title is read closely. Keil and Delitzsch note that the marginal reading and the Chronicles both give the singular, and argue for it on syntactical grounds: had more than one of the men named held that post, their names would most probably have been linked by a conjunction. Ellicott approaches the same question from the history, observing that Joab is elsewhere said to have had ten armour-bearers (2 Samuel 18:15), and suggesting that this one was probably their chief — which would make the singular a statement of rank rather than of number.
38:
The two Ithrites are placed by family rather than by exploit. Gill follows the Targum in deriving the epithet from Jether and makes them descendants of Caleb, of the tribe of Judah; Keil and Delitzsch take the same gentile name but trace it to a family settled in Kirjath-jearim (1 Chronicles 2:53). Keil and Delitzsch add a caution against a natural confusion, that this Ira is of course a different man from the priest of that name mentioned earlier in the book (2 Samuel 20:26).

The last name on the roll needs no explanation and receives almost none. Gill identifies him in four words as the husband of Bathsheba; Keil and Delitzsch say only that Uriah the Hittite is well known from the earlier chapter (2 Samuel 11:3). Neither draws a moral from the position, but neither softens it either: the catalogue of the men who served David best closes with the man he had killed, and the commentary lets that stand without comment.

The closing total is checked by both grammatical commentators, who reach it by different routes. Keil and Delitzsch pronounce the number correct and show the arithmetic — three in the first class, two in the second, and thirty-two in the third — which comes out exact only because they have already amended one verse to yield three names instead of one. Ellicott counts the names as the text gives them and finds only thirty-six, then offers two ways of making up the difference: either the unnamed third member of the second triad is being counted, or the two names the Chronicles has at that same disputed verse should replace the single name here. The two agree, in effect, that the total can be defended but not from the received text alone.

Beyond this list the Chronicles has more. Clarke sets out the sixteen further names appended there — Zabad son of Ahlai, Adina son of Shiza the Reubenite with thirty under him, Hanan son of Maachah, Joshaphat the Mithnite, Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jehiel sons of Hothan the Aroerite, Jediael son of Shimri with his brother Joha the Tizite, Eliel the Mahavite, Jeribai and Joshaviah sons of Elnaam, Ithmah the Moabite, and Eliel, Obed and Jasiel the Mesobaite. Ellicott explains the surplus two ways, as either men who took the places of these heroes as they died or simply other heroes thought worthy of record though hardly reckoned with this particular body.

Clarke then uses the end of the chapter to return to its opening, which he had called very obscure. He reports De Dieu's reading of the fourth and fifth verses, in which David amplifies the perpetuity of his kingdom by comparison with three natural things that are very grateful to men but not constant: the sun rises and goes down again, the morning may be clear but clouds afterwards arise, and the tender grass springs up but afterwards withers. The force of the comparison on that reading is the denial — not so is David's house before God, flourishing like all these but perpetual, because an everlasting covenant has been made with him though some afflictions have befallen him. Clarke notes that De Dieu reaches this by repeating the particle of similitude three times, and closes by directing the reader once more to Kennicott's First Dissertation on the state of the printed Hebrew text, where he holds several corruptions are demonstrated.
